name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
title: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
answer: Shadow AI in legal teams covers the use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals and legal operations staff without the knowledge or approval of the firm's IT, security or general counsel function. It includes personal accounts on public chatbots, browser extensions that summarise or draft text, transcription apps on personal phones, and free or trial tools adopted to speed up research, discovery or contract review. The scope is defined less by the technology than by the absence of a procurement, security or records review, which is what separates it from sanctioned AI use. Because legal work routinely involves privileged, confidential and personal data, even small unsanctioned uses can create obligations the team has not planned for.

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams covers the use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals and legal operations staff without the knowledge or approval of the firm's IT, security or general counsel function. It includes personal accounts on public chatbots, browser extensions that summarise or draft text, transcription apps on personal phones, and free or trial tools adopted to speed up research, discovery or contract review. The scope is defined less by the technology than by the absence of a procurement, security or records review, which is what separates it from sanctioned AI use. Because legal work routinely involves privileged, confidential and personal data, even small unsanctioned uses can create obligations the team has not planned for.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Shadow AI usually runs on the same public cloud services as approved tools, but through individual accounts, personal devices or consumer tiers that sit outside single sign-on, device management and data loss prevention. Files may be pasted into a chat window, uploaded to a summariser, or captured by a meeting recorder that stores audio on a vendor's servers. Some tools run locally in a browser or on a laptop, which limits exposure but also hides the activity from network monitoring. The practical result is that data leaves the firm's controlled environment through channels that IT cannot see, log or delete on request.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Audits for shadow AI typically combine network and endpoint telemetry, expense and procurement records, and interviews with practice groups about what they actually use day to day. Reviewers look for unsanctioned domains in web traffic, personal accounts on managed devices, and AI features embedded in tools the firm already licenses. On the enablement side, teams run short surveys, publish a lightweight intake path for new tools, and stand up a sandbox or approved assistant so that a safe option exists before a ban is announced. The work is iterative, because the tool landscape changes faster than most annual review cycles.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The core risks are confidentiality and privilege, plus data protection duties when client or personnel data is uploaded to a third party without a contract in place. Firms also face records retention and eDiscovery questions when drafts, prompts and outputs live in personal accounts that are not captured by firm systems. Provenance matters: an output that cannot be traced to a source, a model version or a date is hard to rely on in advice or to defend later. Governance responses usually pair a clear acceptable use policy with disclosure expectations, vendor terms review, and training that explains why the rule exists rather than only what is banned. This site tracks 152 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which illustrates why provenance and rights questions are not hypothetical.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect shadow AI to keep shrinking as a purely covert problem and to reappear as a governance gap, because approved assistants will absorb much of the casual use while new tools keep arriving faster than review cycles. Vendors are adding enterprise controls, audit logs and data residency options, which makes approval cheaper and bans less necessary.The teams that fare best tend to treat enablement and monitoring as one programme rather than two, so that lawyers have a fast, safe route to the tools they want.
